tips: Watch for the repeated heading "These are the generations of…" (Genesis 2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 11:27; 37:2). It divides the book into family histories and shows the story narrowing from all humanity to one chosen family.
Read chapters 1–11 as the backdrop and chapters 12–50 as God's answer: the promise to Abraham of land, descendants, and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3) drives everything that follows.
Notice how often the younger son is chosen over the older—Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim. Genesis repeatedly shows God working through unlikely people rather than expected ones.

looksAhead.title: The promise to Abraham
looksAhead.text: God's promise that all families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3) is picked up by Paul, who calls it the gospel preached in advance (Galatians 3:8).

looksAhead.title: From Eden to the new creation
looksAhead.text: The tree of life, lost in Genesis 3:22–24, reappears in the final chapters of the Bible, where the curse is removed (Revelation 22:1–3).

looksAhead.title: Into Egypt
looksAhead.text: Genesis ends with Jacob's family settled in Egypt (Genesis 50:22–26), setting the stage for their slavery and rescue in Exodus.

tips: The book moves in three settings: Egypt (chapters 1–15), the journey to Sinai (15–18), and Mount Sinai (19–40). Keep track of where Israel is; each setting shows a different side of God.
Don't skim the tabernacle chapters (25–31; 35–40). Their point is that the God who rescued Israel now wants to live among them, and the long, careful instructions show how seriously that is taken.

Read the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20) in light of their opening line: "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt." The law is given to people already rescued, not as a way to earn rescue.

looksBack.title: God remembers his covenant
looksBack.text: Israel's rescue happens because "God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob" (Exodus 2:24), fulfilling the promise of Genesis 15:13–14.

looksAhead.title: The Passover lamb
looksAhead.text: The Passover (Exodus 12) becomes a picture of Jesus' death: Paul writes that "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

looksAhead.title: God dwelling with his people
looksAhead.text: The glory filling the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35) is echoed when John says the Word "dwelt among us" (John 1:14), and in the promise that God will dwell with his people forever (Revelation 21:3).

tips: Remember where Israel is: camped at Sinai with God's presence now in the tabernacle in their midst. Leviticus answers one question—how can sinful people live near a holy God?

Look for the book's key word, holy, and its central refrain: "ye shall be holy; for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44). The laws about food, skin disease, and cleanliness all teach Israel to be different from the nations around them.
Chapter 16, the Day of Atonement, is the book's center. Read it carefully before and after the surrounding laws; it shows how the whole system dealt with sin.

looksBack.title: The tabernacle completed
looksBack.text: Leviticus begins where Exodus ends: the LORD speaks to Moses "out of the tabernacle" (Leviticus 1:1) that had just been filled with his glory (Exodus 40:34–35).

looksAhead.title: The Day of Atonement
looksAhead.text: Hebrews explains the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) as a shadow of Christ, who entered the true holy place "by his own blood" once for all (Hebrews 9:11–12).

looksAhead.title: Love your neighbour
looksAhead.text: Jesus names Leviticus 19:18, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," as the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39).

tips: The book is named for its two censuses (chapters 1 and 26). The first counts the generation that left Egypt; the second counts their children. What happens between them explains why only the second group entered the land.
Read chapters 13–14 as the turning point. The people's refusal to enter Canaan turns an eleven-day journey into forty years in the wilderness.
Watch the pattern of complaint and judgment, and notice God's faithfulness despite it—including the surprising blessings spoken through the hired prophet Balaam (chapters 22–24).

looksBack.title: Leaving Sinai
looksBack.text: Numbers picks up after the law is given and the tabernacle is built, as Israel organizes to leave Mount Sinai (Numbers 10:11–12).

looksAhead.title: Warnings for later readers
looksAhead.text: Paul says the wilderness failures "happened unto them for ensamples" and were written to warn believers (1 Corinthians 10:1–11); Hebrews 3:7–19 makes the same point.

looksAhead.title: The serpent lifted up
looksAhead.text: Jesus compares his death to the bronze serpent Moses lifted up in the wilderness (Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14–15).

tips: Read it as a series of farewell sermons. Moses is speaking to the new generation on the edge of the Promised Land, retelling the journey and urging them to choose faithfulness.
Notice the book's emotional heart in the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Obedience flows from love, not fear.
Pay attention to the blessings and curses (chapters 27–30). The rest of Israel's history in Joshua through 2 Kings is measured against them.

looksBack.title: Retelling the wilderness years
looksBack.text: Moses reviews the journey from Horeb (Sinai) recounted in Numbers, including the failure at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 1:19–46; Numbers 13–14).

looksAhead.title: Jesus answers temptation
looksAhead.text: Each time Jesus is tempted in the wilderness, he answers with words from Deuteronomy (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10; Deuteronomy 8:3; 6:16; 6:13).

looksAhead.title: The standard for Israel's kings
looksAhead.text: The law for kings (Deuteronomy 17:14–20) becomes the measure of Israel's monarchy; Solomon breaks it by multiplying horses, wives, and gold (1 Kings 10:26–11:4).

looksAhead.title: A prophet like Moses
looksAhead.text: The promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15) is applied to Jesus by Peter (Acts 3:22–26).
